what_it_does: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) is a technique that lets a computer perform calculations directly on encrypted data — the data stays scrambled the entire time, so the server never sees the raw values. The catch is that each multiplication operation on encrypted numbers gradually degrades the data's integrity (the technical term is 'consuming noise budget' or 'draining levels'); once the budget is exhausted, the encrypted result is unreadable. To fix this, you run a reset operation called 'bootstrapping,' which is very expensive in time and compute. Deciding exactly where in a program to insert these resets has been automated by compilers, but prior tools could not handle loops — a fundamental building block of almost every real program. HALO is a compiler that extends automatic reset-placement to programs with loops by analyzing how the noise budget evolves across loop iterations and finding the minimum number of resets needed to keep the budget from running out, inserting them only where necessary.
